issue.issue_text: Whether imposing a sentence of ‘imprisonment till the rising of the court’ is permissible and intra vires, especially when the penal provision (Section 494 IPC) prescribes no minimum imprisonment.

law.fact_text: The proviso to Section 418(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) explicitly recognizes the sentence of 'imprisonment till the rising of the Court', treating it as a form of simple imprisonment.
The penal provision for bigamy, Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), prescribes a maximum term of imprisonment but does not set any minimum term.

The Court noted a historical conflict in judicial opinion, where some earlier High Court decisions considered this sentence an evasion of the law, but later decisions held that courts have full discretion when no minimum sentence is prescribed.

application.fact_text: The Court reasoned that the explicit mention of this sentence in the proviso to Section 418(1) Cr.P.C. confirms its legal validity.
application.application_text: The Court relied on the statutory recognition of the sentence within the Cr.P.C. itself.

application.fact_text: The Court combined this statutory recognition with the fact that Section 494 IPC provides no minimum sentence.
application.application_text: The absence of a minimum sentence in the penal provision grants the court wide discretion in determining the length of imprisonment, which can include a very short period like 'till the rising of the court'.

application.fact_text: Based on these two points, the Court concluded that imposing such a sentence is not an evasion of the law but a legally valid exercise of judicial discretion.
application.application_text: The combination of the procedural law (Cr.P.C.) acknowledging the sentence and the substantive penal law (IPC) allowing for discretion makes the sentence legally permissible.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a sentence of 'imprisonment till the rising of the court' is permissible and intra vires. This conclusion was based on the combined effect of the proviso to Section 418(1) Cr.P.C., which statutorily recognizes this form of sentence, and the fact that the relevant penal provision, Section 494 IPC, prescribes no minimum term of imprisonment, thereby giving the court discretion.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Following the rule of proportionality in imposing punishment would promote and bring order and orderliness in society.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When an offence under Section 494 I.P.C. is found to be a serious offence, the imposition of a sentence of ‘imprisonment till the rising of the court’ is not a proper sentence because it is not in tune with the rule of proportionality in providing punishment.
legal_tests_applied: The rule of proportionality in providing punishment, which requires that a sentence be adequate, just, and commensurate with the gravity, nature of the crime, and the manner in which the offence is committed.
The court has a solemn duty to strike a proper balance while awarding a sentence, considering the social interest and conscience of the society.
policy_considerations: The demand for deserved punishment proportionate to the gravity of the offence is a continuous one based on civic sense, and failing to apply the rule of proportionality will impact society.
The punishment should not be so lenient that it shocks the conscience of the society.
Imposing an inadequate sentence out of undue sympathy does more harm to the justice system and undermines public confidence in the efficacy of law.
Awarding a lesser sentence encourages criminals, which in turn causes society to suffer.
Following the rule of proportionality in imposing punishment promotes and brings order and orderliness to society.
